title: Security & Compliance Control Book: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, Risk & Exceptions
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's operational controls and workflows for access control (RBAC & auth), audit logging, data residency and retention, a secure SDLC, incident response for security events, compliance evidence collection, and risk & exception handling. It is intended for engineers, SREs, product managers, and security reviewers responsible for designing and operating customer-facing and internal services.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood-managed services (hosted API, dedicated, private) and developer tooling (console, CLI, infra pipelines).
- Excludes third-party SaaS (see vendor risk register for specifics).

Ownership and Contacts:
- Primary owner: Security (security@redwood.ai).
- Service owners: runtime-team@redwood.ai, infra-team@redwood.ai, platform-team@redwood.ai.
- Evidence and audit contact: compliance-ops@redwood.ai.

1) RBAC & Authentication
- Systems: redwood-auth (OIDC provider gateway), IAM service (internal role mapping), and customer-bound roles for Dedicated/Private.
- Principles: least privilege, role-based access, separation of duties, and just-in-time elevation for emergency ops.
- Role matrix (examples):
  - infra-admin: full terraform and cloud account actions (owner: infra-team)
  - runtime-operator: deploy/run inference clusters, read logs (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
  - support-analyst: read-only customer metadata, create support tickets (owner: customer-success)
  - auditor: read-only access to audit logs and config (owner: security)
- Provisioning:
  1. All role assignments must be requested via the access-request form in Confluence (link in related pages) and approved by role owner.
  2. Automation: use IAM provisioning pipeline (cli: redwood-iam grant --role runtime-operator --user <email>).
- Periodic review: quarterly entitlement review with automated reports. High-risk roles (infra-admin, infra-billing) reviewed monthly.
- Authentication: OIDC via corporate IdP with MFA required for all human users. Service-to-service uses short-lived mTLS certificates or signed JWTs issued by redwood-auth.

2) Audit Logging
- Architecture: All services emit structured JSON logs to log-ingest (rsyslog/FluentD -> internal Kafka -> log-store). redwood-audit collects auth, privilege changes, and provisioning events. Critical sources: CloudTrail (AWS), GCP audit logs, application auth events, infra pipeline events.
- Required log fields: timestamp, service, instance_id, environment, user_id/service_id, action, resource, request_id, ip, outcome, trace_id.
- SLOs and thresholds:
  - Log collection latency: 99th percentile <= 2 minutes from event to index.
  - Retention alerts: when ingestion backlog > 1 hour create paged alert.
  - Security alert rule: > 100 auth failures for a single user in 5m triggers high-priority incident.
- Retention and access:
  - Default retention: 2 years (index), 7 years (cold archive for enterprise customers on request).
  - Access control: only auditor and security roles can access raw auth logs. All access to logs is logged and reviewed monthly.
- Forensics: preserve full context (request payloads, traces) for 90 days hot, then compressed archive.

3) Data Residency & Retention
- Policy: workloads are hosted in customer-chosen regions where possible. Services have region tagging: eu-west-1, us-west-2, ap-southeast-1.
- Default retention table (by data class):
  - Customer PII: retention configurable, default 2 years, minimum purge after 90 days if requested.
  - Audit logs: 2 years index, 7 years archive (enterprise opt-in).
  - Model artifacts: 5 years unless marked ephemeral.
  - Metrics/telemetry: 13 months detailed, aggregated 5 years.
- Data deletion: documented KMS-wrapped keys and S3 lifecycle policies. To request cross-region migration or deletion, open a ticket with compliance-ops with customer approval.

4) Secure SDLC
- Stages: design -> implement -> test -> pre-prod -> deploy -> monitor.
- Requirements:
  - Mandatory code review for all PRs; at least one reviewer from different team for infra changes.
  - Static Analysis: all PRs must pass SAST and dependency-scan (Snyk/OSS audit).
  - Secrets: forbid plaintext secrets in repos. Use Vault and environment secret encryption.
  - CI gates: unit tests, integration tests, chaos test for runtime components, and canary promotion.
- Release controls: change window, rollback playbook, feature flags for canary. For high-risk changes (auth, audit, encryption), a security review is required and must be documented in the PR template.

5) Incident Response (Security) Procedures
- Detection and triage:
  1. Alerts from IDS/EDR/Datadog/Log ruleland to #sec-ops and PagerDuty.
  2. Triage lead assigns severity (P1-P4) within 15 minutes.
- Key steps for P1 (compromise, data exfiltration):
  1. Contain: revoke affected keys, isolate pods/hosts, suspend relevant services.
  2. Preserve evidence: snapshot volumes, export full audit logs, record timeline.
  3. Communicate: notify CTO, legal, customer-success for impacted customers, and follow notification SLA.
  4. Remediate: patch, rotate keys, and perform root cause analysis.
  5. Post-incident: publish postmortem within 7 days (redacted if required) and remediation tracker.
- Playbooks: link to service-specific runbooks (runbooks and incident-process directories).

6) Compliance Evidence & Audit Workflows
- Evidence store: evidence-store (S3 bucket, access audit via AWS CloudTrail and encrypted with KMS).
- Common artifacts and owners:
  - RBAC entitlement exports (owner: security)
  - Audit log retention reports (owner: infra-team)
  - SDLC evidence: PR reviews, SAST reports (owner: eng-developer-experience)
  - Incident records and postmortems (owner: oncall-and-incident-response)
- Workflow for external audit:
  1. Pre-audit: compliance-ops prepare evidence bundle and map to control IDs.
  2. Access: auditors receive time-limited access to evidence-store and a working directory in Confluence.
  3. Follow-up: artifacts delivered and signed attestation, remediation plan tracked in the compliance tracker.
- Automation: scheduled evidence exports for SOC2/ISO audits; compliance-ops owns schedule and proof-of-access logs.

7) Risk & Exceptions
- Exception process:
  1. Submit Risk & Exception Form (Confluence template) with scope, compensating controls, and risk owner.
  2. Security reviews and assigns risk rating (Low/Medium/High).
  3. Approval: High-risk exceptions require CISO sign-off and executive sponsor; medium-risk exceptions require security director sign-off.
  4. Mitigation plan and expiry: every exception must include a mitigation plan and an expiry date (max 90 days for high-risk).
- Example acceptance criteria: temporary access to customer data for migration with recorded session, MFA enforced, and time-limited credentials.
- Risk register: maintained by security and reviewed in quarterly risk committee.

Appendices and Examples:
- Example RBAC JSON policy (CLI snippet):
  {
    "role": "runtime-operator",
    "actions": ["deploy:create","deploy:update","logs:read"],
    "resources": ["cluster/*"]
  }
- Sample log query (Datadog):
  service:redwood-auth AND status:error AND @user.email:"*@example.com" | count by @user.email
- Incident command example (CLI):
  # revoke all active service tokens for service-id
  redwood-auth revoke --service service-id --reason "Compromise containment"

Maintenance and Review:
- This document is reviewed annually and after every P1 security incident. Owners listed above are responsible for updates.
